cards.explanation: The answer is bless the LORD. David, Israel's king, says, "I will bless the LORD at all times; His praise will always be on my lips." The title says this song comes from the time he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, the king who drove him away. Notice the song doesn't open with a complaint about that day. At all times means the LORD gets the song even then, and I'd have been tempted to write a strongly worded letter.

The answer is rejoice. David says, "let the oppressed hear and rejoice." The oppressed are people being pressed down, and he wants them to hear his boast in the LORD and be glad. A boast that lifts people up is the best kind to pass along.
The answer is False. David says, "Magnify the LORD with me; let us exalt His name together." He's not keeping it to himself, friends. He's passing out invitations, and I'd have been first in line.

The answer is True. David says, "I sought the LORD, and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears." Notice that the word is all. He doesn't say some of them or the small ones. That's David telling what happened when he sought the LORD.

The answer is joy. David says, "Those who look to Him are radiant with joy; their faces shall never be ashamed." Radiant means glowing, so you can see it on their faces. I think that's a better glow than anything an oven gives off.

The answer is False. David says, "This poor man called out, and the LORD heard him; He saved him from all his troubles." Not some of them, ALL of them. I was in a 25 cent bin and I'd take that deal in a heartbeat.

The answer is around those who fear Him. David says, "The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them." Encamps means pitching a camp, like a guard setting up right around you. I think that's about as close as protection gets.

The answer is that He is good. David says, "Taste and see that the LORD is good; blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him!" Tasting is firsthand, not hearsay. You can't know what a fresh cookie is like by hearing about it, so I think David is inviting us all to come find out for ourselves.

The answer is nothing. David says, "Fear the LORD, you His saints, for those who fear Him lack nothing." Nothing means nothing, friends. Saints are God's holy people, and David is talking to them directly. I have never once seen my pantry that full.

The answer is that young lions go lacking and hungry. David says, "Young lions go lacking and hungry, but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing." Young lions are strong hunters, and they still go without. The ones who seek the LORD lack no good thing. I think the point is that strength alone doesn't fill the plate.

The answer is keep your tongue from evil. David asks who wants good days, and the first answer is "Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceitful speech." It starts with what comes out of your mouth. I'll be honest, I've said a few things to my own cookie dough that I'd take back.
The answer is False. David says, "Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it." He gives us two verbs for one job, seek and pursue. I think that tells us peace is worth the chase.

The answer is cry. David says, "The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their cry." Inclined means leaning in to listen. The LORD isn't just looking, friends, He's listening too.

The answer is that the memory of them is wiped from the earth. David says, "…the face of the LORD is against those who do evil, to wipe out all memory of them from the earth." That's a heavy line, and it's good to say so plainly. It sits right beside the verse where the LORD's eyes are on the righteous (Psalm 34:15).
The answer is True. David says, "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit." Near is a good word to hold onto. I think this verse is one to read slowly.

The answer is False. David says, "Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all." Notice he says many, not none. And the word all shows up again, just like it did earlier in the song.
The answer is broken. David says, "He protects all his bones; not one of them will be broken." That's a very specific kind of care. Every single bone, and not one is missed.

The answer is that they will be condemned. David says, "Evil will slay the wicked, and the haters of the righteous will be condemned." That's a heavy line, and the word is condemned. Right after it, David says, "The LORD redeems His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned." (Psalm 34:22)

The answer is redeems. David ends with, "The LORD redeems His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned." Redeems is the word he closes on. The song ends with the LORD's servants and those who take refuge in Him.
